title: Harvard scientist pushes back on NASA chief over mystery space object: 'It's not an asteroid'
excerpt: Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb says near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26 is "not an asteroid," pushing back on NASA chief Jared Isaacman and arguing it could be a lost Soviet spacecraft.
content:

A Harvard astrophysicist behind the theory that a mysterious object speeding through the solar system could actually be a lost Soviet spacecraft is pushing back on NASA's top official, saying the object is "not an asteroid."

Known as 1998 KY26, the roughly 36-foot-wide object is believed to be a near-Earth asteroid but is accelerating in a way gravity alone cannot explain. Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb and his colleagues have examined whether it could instead be Phobos 1, a Soviet spacecraft that stopped communicating while traveling to Mars in 1988.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman weighed in on the mysterious object Thursday during an appearance on "Fox & Friends."

EIFFEL TOWER-SIZED ASTEROID APOPHIS TO PASS CLOSER TO EARTH THAN MANY SATELLITES IN 2029, NASA SAYS

"I've not seen any evidence to suggest this is...anything other than an asteroid," Isaacman said.

Two shape models show scientists' estimates of the form of near-Earth object 1998 KY26. (Credit: NASA)

Loeb challenged that assessment during an interview with Fox News Digital on Friday.

HARVARD ASTRONOMER TAPPED TO LEAD WHITE HOUSE UFO COUNCIL SAYS US GOVERNMENT 'BAFFLED BY WHAT THEY ARE SEEING'

"Well, first of all, it's not an asteroid because 1998 KY26 appears to have non-gravitational acceleration, meaning it's being pushed by some force other than gravity, and asteroids are just rocks," Loeb said.

Scientists have been trying to explain what is causing the additional acceleration.

SCIENTISTS DISCOVER POTENTIALLY MASSIVE DWARF PLANET CANDIDATE HIDING BEYOND PLUTO

One theory has been that KY26 is a "dark comet," a rocky object behaving like a comet without producing a visible cloud or tail.

An illustration shows the Soviet Phobos 1 spacecraft, which was launched toward Mars in July 1988 but lost after a faulty command caused it to shut down. (Credit: NASA)

New research from Georgia Tech has cast doubt on whether KY26 could retain enough ice to produce that effect, while other research has suggested pressure from sunlight and heat radiating from its surface could account for the acceleration.

GIANT ROBOTIC CLAWS WILL GRAB DEAD SATELLITES IN SPACE

Loeb told Fox News Digital that his team found KY26's trajectory closely resembles that of the failed Soviet mission and calculated that sunlight reflecting off Phobos 1 could produce a push consistent with the nongravitational acceleration observed in KY26.

He also pointed to recent observations indicating the object is highly reflective and rotates about once every five minutes.

A model of Phobos 1, the Soviet spacecraft that lost contact with Earth while traveling to Mars in 1988. Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb and his colleagues have examined whether the mysterious object 1998 KY26 could be the lost probe. (Credit: NASA)

NASA'S CHANDRA TELESCOPE REVEALS MILKY WAY'S OUTER REACHES MAY STRETCH FARTHER THAN PREVIOUSLY KNOWN

The lack of a visible cometary tail or evidence of material escaping the object is central to Loeb's skepticism of the dark-comet explanation.

"It could be a comet shedding some gas backward that is pushing it forward, but in that case we should have seen the gas," Loeb said. "We should have seen the dust because for comets we see a tail and the dust particles are being pushed away from the sun by the solar radiation."

"We don't see a cometary tail. We don't see any evidence for outgassing around this object. That's the puzzle," he added.

Loeb compared the debate over how to classify KY26 to encountering an unfamiliar animal at a zoo.

"If you are an expert on zebras and you see an elephant, you would say the elephant is a zebra without stripes," Loeb said. "But that's an oxymoron because it's a completely different animal."

He also argued that scientists should be willing to consider explanations outside the familiar categories of asteroids and comets when observations do not neatly fit either one.

"Innovation in science requires some imagination," Loeb said. "It requires you to allow for the possibility that our knowledge is incomplete."
